scenes.tts: After D N A is copied, why do daughter cells not simply forget which genes were silent? The first film showed that access and regulators shape output. Now follow one regulatory state through replication and division. The sequence survives, but the state still needs maintenance.
scenes.caption: After DNA is copied, why do daughter cells not simply forget which genes were silent? The first film showed that access and regulators shape output. Now follow one regulatory state through replication and division. The sequence survives, but the state still needs maintenance.
scenes.visual: Resume the first film's 16:9 liver-cell nucleus without a reset. Reuse its exact colour map: BLUE DNA, GOLD nucleosomes, WHITE promoter, TEAL enhancer, GREEN regulators, MAGENTA DNA-methylation tags, pale-grey RNA. The same large schematic gene fills over sixty percent of frame height. Its promoter carries several magenta tags and releases little RNA. As the question appears, a cell-division line begins forming through the nucleus. Keep 'schematic' visible.
scenes.narration: After DNA is copied, why do daughter cells not simply forget which genes were silent? The first film showed that access and regulators shape output. Now follow one regulatory state through replication and division. The sequence survives, but the state still needs maintenance.

scenes.visual: Fade in the title 'Rebuilding the Memory' above the carried blue DNA ribbon. Gold nucleosomes drift gently, magenta tags pulse, and the cell-division line advances slightly. Fade the title before replication begins.

scenes.tts: Replication copies the D N A sequence. It does not automatically place every chemical mark on both new molecules. Look at a methylated C p G site, where a C is followed by a G. Each daughter duplex first has one old marked strand. Its partner is a new unmarked strand.
scenes.caption: Replication copies the DNA sequence. It does not automatically place every chemical mark on both new molecules. Look at a methylated CpG site, where a C is followed by a G. Each daughter duplex first has one old marked strand. Its partner is a new unmarked strand.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the blue ribbon as it separates into two template strands. New blue partner strands grow beside them from left to right. Keep magenta tags on the old strands only. Mark each strand clearly 'old' or 'new' with large labels. Do not draw bases or molecular structures; use paired parallel ribbons and labelled positions. A small legend reads 'magenta tag = methylated CpG, schematic'.
scenes.narration: Replication copies the DNA sequence. It does not automatically place every chemical mark on both new molecules. Look at a methylated CpG site, where a C is followed by a G. Each daughter duplex first has one old marked strand. Its partner is a new unmarked strand.

scenes.tts: The two strands now differ at each marked site. One carries inherited positional information. The other carries freshly copied sequence. A maintenance system must distinguish them before both daughter molecules can regain a similar pattern.
scenes.caption: The two strands now differ at each marked site. One carries inherited positional information. The other carries freshly copied sequence. A maintenance system must distinguish them before both daughter molecules can regain a similar pattern.
scenes.visual: Hold two enlarged paired BLUE ribbons side by side. On each, one old strand carries MAGENTA tags and one new strand has none. Animate a large bracket between the alternatives 'old marked strand' and 'new unmarked strand'. A question mark travels between them while the matching CpG position markers stay aligned. Do not introduce DNMT1 yet.
scenes.narration: The two strands now differ at each marked site. One carries inherited positional information. The other carries freshly copied sequence. A maintenance system must distinguish them before both daughter molecules can regain a similar pattern.

scenes.tts: Now predict. Which strand can guide restoration of the methylation pattern: the old marked strand or the new unmarked strand? Hold both possibilities beside the same C p G positions.
scenes.caption: Now predict. Which strand can guide restoration of the methylation pattern: the old marked strand or the new unmarked strand? Hold both possibilities beside the same CpG positions.
scenes.visual: Enlarge the two answer paths: 'old marked strand?' and 'new unmarked strand?' Keep both beside the same aligned CpG position markers. The question 'Which strand guides restoration?' fills the upper third. MAGENTA tags pulse on the old strand while the new strand remains unmarked; do not highlight an answer.
scenes.narration: Now predict. Which strand can guide restoration of the methylation pattern: the old marked strand or the new unmarked strand? Hold both possibilities beside the same CpG positions.

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Hold 'Which strand guides restoration?' with both answer paths equally bright. The paired blue ribbons drift slowly, while magenta tags stay fixed on old strands. Do not introduce DNMT1 or reveal an answer.

scenes.tts: The old marked strand supplies the template. Guided to these half-marked sites, D N M T one copies the old pattern onto the new strand. It is the main maintenance enzyme here. Other methyltransferases lay down new patterns.
scenes.caption: The old marked strand supplies the template. Guided to these half-marked sites, DNMT1 copies the old pattern onto the new strand. It is the main maintenance enzyme here. Other methyltransferases lay down new patterns.
scenes.visual: Highlight 'old marked strand' and fade the alternative. A large GREEN block labelled 'DNMT1' travels along each paired BLUE ribbon. It is drawn to half-marked sites; whenever it reaches an old-strand MAGENTA tag, a matching magenta tag appears opposite on the new strand. Keep additions synchronized with narration. A restrained heading reads 'maintenance methylation'. Show a separate small label 'new patterns: other methyltransferases' without animating a de novo mechanism.
scenes.narration: The old marked strand supplies the template. Guided to these half-marked sites, DNMT1 copies the old pattern onto the new strand. It is the main maintenance enzyme here. Other methyltransferases lay down new patterns.

scenes.tts: In mammals, dense methylation of a promoter C p G island goes with a silent gene, within promoter-specific limits. A restored pattern can therefore help keep that promoter quiet in both daughters.
scenes.caption: In mammals, dense methylation of a promoter CpG island goes with a silent gene, within promoter-specific limits. A restored pattern can therefore help keep that promoter quiet in both daughters.
scenes.visual: Return to one enlarged promoter. Several MAGENTA tags cluster near the WHITE promoter, labelled 'dense promoter CpG methylation'. The RNA stream becomes smaller but does not receive a crossed-out symbol. Keep the qualifier 'goes with silence; promoter-specific limits'. Do not show MeCP2 or deacetylases; the lesson text covers that link.
scenes.narration: In mammals, dense methylation of a promoter CpG island goes with a silent gene, within promoter-specific limits. A restored pattern can therefore help keep that promoter quiet in both daughters.

scenes.tts: When the pattern is restored after replication, both daughters can inherit a similar regulatory state. That does not guarantee identical expression. It helps preserve the conditions under which the gene remains hard to read. Similar does not mean perfectly fixed.
scenes.caption: When the pattern is restored after replication, both daughters can inherit a similar regulatory state. That does not guarantee identical expression. It helps preserve the conditions under which the gene remains hard to read. Similar does not mean perfectly fixed.
scenes.visual: Replay maintenance correctly: the GREEN DNMT1 block restores matching MAGENTA tags on new strands. Divide the nucleus into two daughter cells. Each receives a similarly tagged copy of the gene. Their RNA readouts remain low but gently fluctuate at different levels. Show 'helps preserve' between them, not an equals sign.
scenes.narration: When the pattern is restored after replication, both daughters can inherit a similar regulatory state. That does not guarantee identical expression. It helps preserve the conditions under which the gene remains hard to read. Similar does not mean perfectly fixed.

scenes.tts: An epigenetic change is inherited across cell divisions without changing D N A sequence. Mitotic inheritance is well established through D N M T one and more. X inactivation and imprinting can keep one gene copy silent through many divisions.
scenes.caption: An epigenetic change is inherited across cell divisions without changing DNA sequence. Mitotic inheritance is well established through DNMT1 and more. X inactivation and imprinting can keep one gene copy silent through many divisions.
scenes.visual: The two daughter cells become a branching lineage tree. BLUE DNA ribbons remain the same length and order in every branch, while one of two WHITE gene-copy slots stays dim. Add two large example labels in sequence, 'X inactivation' and 'imprinting'. A bracket under the tree reads 'mitotic inheritance: established'. Keep motion in the branching line and drifting nucleosomes.
scenes.narration: An epigenetic change is inherited across cell divisions without changing DNA sequence. Mitotic inheritance is well established through DNMT1 and more. X inactivation and imprinting can keep one gene copy silent through many divisions.

scenes.tts: Inheritance through a whole animal's germline is a different claim. It is documented in plants and in C elegans. In mammals, most D N A methylation is erased and rewritten in developing germ cells and in the early embryo. That is one reason transgenerational claims remain limited and contested.
scenes.caption: Inheritance through a whole animal's germline is a different claim. It is documented in plants and in C. elegans. In mammals, most DNA methylation is erased and rewritten in developing germ cells and in the early embryo. That is one reason transgenerational claims remain limited and contested.
scenes.visual: Move the mitotic lineage tree left. On the right, build a separate path labelled 'germline across generations'. A plant icon and a simple worm silhouette receive solid evidence brackets. A mammal silhouette receives a dashed bracket labelled 'limited and contested'. Along the mammal path, many MAGENTA tags fade and later reappear in changed positions, labelled 'most methylation erased and rewritten: germ cells, early embryo' and a small tag 'one reason'.
scenes.narration: Inheritance through a whole animal's germline is a different claim. It is documented in plants and in C. elegans. In mammals, most DNA methylation is erased and rewritten in developing germ cells and in the early embryo. That is one reason transgenerational claims remain limited and contested.

scenes.tts: So chemical marks are not permanent ink. Maintenance machinery must restore a state after replication, and other regulators can oppose it. Cellular memory is an active process. Replication creates the need again each time. It is not evidence that every acquired state crosses generations.
scenes.caption: So chemical marks are not permanent ink. Maintenance machinery must restore a state after replication, and other regulators can oppose it. Cellular memory is an active process. Replication creates the need again each time. It is not evidence that every acquired state crosses generations.
scenes.visual: Transform a static ink-bottle icon into moving maintenance machinery around the carried gene. GREEN maintenance blocks add MAGENTA tags. The MAGENTA tags stay in place while a separate GREEN-outlined activator competes at the promoter and the RNA readout rises modestly, showing opposition without choosing a universal outcome; no tag disappears. Pull back to mitotic daughters on the left and the dashed mammalian germline path on the right. Place 'active rebuilding' over only the mitotic branch.
scenes.narration: So chemical marks are not permanent ink. Maintenance machinery must restore a state after replication, and other regulators can oppose it. Cellular memory is an active process. Replication creates the need again each time. It is not evidence that every acquired state crosses generations.

scenes.visual: End card with one line only: 'Cell memory requires regulatory states to be propagated or restored after replication.' Behind it, one blue DNA ribbon duplicates and receives matching magenta tags through a slow pass of the green DNMT1 block. Show no subtitle, logo, or second line.
